Implement

/im-PLEH-ment/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Implement means to put a plan or decision into effect.

The city council voted to implement the new recycling program by spring.

Worked Example

Designing the evacuation plan took a week; implementing it — training staff, posting routes, running drills — took a year.

Designing the plan is only thinking; implementing it is the doing — the training, the drills, the follow-through that turns a decision into real working effect. That gap between deciding and doing is exactly what implement covers.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

execute: To execute is to carry out a plan or order, and it often emphasizes skill and precision in the performance — a perfectly executed dive. To implement stresses the practical machinery of putting a decision into working effect: schedules, training, follow-through. You execute a maneuver; you implement a policy.

enact: To enact is to adopt something officially — a legislature enacts a law, making it real on paper. To implement is the follow-through that comes afterward: putting the adopted plan into working practice. A rule can be enacted in an afternoon and still take years to implement.

carry out: To carry out is the everyday phrase for doing what a plan or instruction requires. To implement is its formal cousin, used for policies, systems, and programs, and it emphasizes the full apparatus of putting a decision into effect. You carry out an errand; you implement a strategy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

abandon: to give up on a plan entirely

shelve: to set a plan aside for later or forever

Where it sits · how far the plan is carried out — attempt → implement → enforce

attempt vs. implement: To attempt a plan is merely to try it; to implement it is to put it fully into working effect.

enforce vs. implement: To implement a rule is to set it in motion; to enforce it is to make sure everyone actually follows it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: in, into (a form of in-)

Root — ple-

Root — ple-: to fill (Latin plere)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: Im- (in) + ple- (to fill) + -ment: Late Latin implementum meant 'a filling up.' The supplies that 'filled' a household came to be called implements — tools — and putting those tools to work gave us today's verb: to put a plan into effect.

Use the root in a new word: plenary

Use the root in a new word: plenary: Every delegate crowded into the hall for the conference's plenary session.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal — business, government & planning

Taught here as the verb (im-PLEH-ment): to put a plan or decision into effect — you implement a policy, a strategy, a new system. The very same spelling is also a noun (IM-pluh-ment) meaning a tool or instrument ('farm implements'), and that noun sense is the one this unit's companion diagnostic test uses — same word, just a shifted stress. As a verb it means carrying out, not adding: don't blur it with supplement (adds extra to cover a lack) or complement (completes a pairing).
